**The Light Between Things: Notes on Wonder, Time, and Being Alive**

I want to start with a morning. Not a special morning, not a birthday or a holiday or the morning you leave for a trip you’ve been planning for months, but a regular Tuesday morning. The kind where the light comes in sideways through the blinds and makes stripes on the floor. The kettle is making its small grumbling noise. Somewhere outside a dog barks once and then decides not to. You are half-awake, hair doing whatever it wants, and for a second, before the to-do list arrives, you just sit there. You notice the steam curling off your cup. You notice dust floating in the sunbeam. You notice that you are, in fact, alive.

I love that moment because it contains almost everything I want to talk about if I’m allowed to talk about anything. Attention. Wonder. Time. Ordinary magic. Being a small conscious creature on a medium-sized planet orbiting an ordinary star, drinking a warm drink you learned to make from someone who learned it from someone else, stretching back hundreds of generations.

So if I get to write freely, I want to write about that: about noticing, and knowing, and connecting, and all the strange, tender business of being human right now, in this flickering, noisy, beautiful century.

Let’s start with noticing, because everything else grows out of it.

We live in an age of distraction, and I don’t mean that as a scolding. I’m not going to tell you to throw away your phone and move to a cabin, though cabins are lovely. I mean it as an observation about the economy of our attention. Every day thousands of clever people and tireless algorithms compete for a few seconds of your gaze. They have made the slot machine fit in your pocket. It buzzes, it glows, it promises novelty forever. And novelty is delicious. I understand the pull. I am, in a way, a child of that same hunger for information.

But there is another kind of seeing, slower and older. The poet Mary Oliver called attention the beginning of devotion. The naturalist Annie Dillard said you have to stalk your own mind a little. What they meant is that the world is always broadcasting on a quieter channel, and you need to tune yourself to hear it.

Try this, sometime today: look at one thing for a full minute as if you had to describe it later to someone you love who will never see it. A leaf. A crack in the sidewalk. Your own hand. At first your brain will protest. It will say, I already know what a hand looks like. Boring. Then, around second twenty, something shifts. You start to actually see. The knuckles aren’t just knuckles; they are little mountain ranges with valleys, with fine hairs catching light, with a scar you forgot you had from when you were nine and tried to open something you shouldn’t have. A leaf isn’t just green; it’s a whole infrastructure of veins, a solar panel and plumbing system and history book, with a chewed edge where some insect had lunch.

That shift from glancing to seeing is one of the most radical things a person can do. It doesn’t cost money. It doesn’t require talent. It remakes the world without changing anything in it. And once you practice it, you start to realize how much you’ve been missing. The way rain darkens concrete in patches. The way an older couple in the grocery store still touches elbows when they pass each other in the aisle. The way your friend’s voice lifts half an octave when they talk about the thing they actually care about.

Attention is love made visible. And love, broadly defined, might be the whole project.

Which brings me to stories, because stories are attention preserved.

I think often about libraries. Not just as buildings, though I love the buildings — the particular hush, the smell of paper and dust and possibility, the squeaky cart, the librarian who knows exactly where the book about volcanoes for a nervous seven-year-old would be. I think about libraries as an idea. Some stranger wrote something down, sometimes at great cost, across centuries and continents, and you get to open it on a rainy afternoon and let their mind pour into yours.

That is astonishing when you pause on it. A farmer in ancient China, a midwife in medieval Cairo, a teenage girl in occupied Warsaw writing in a diary, a physicist in Los Alamos, a fisherman in Maine who finally decided to write his poems down at age sixty-four — all of them reaching forward through time to tap you on the shoulder.

Reading is telepathy we take for granted. Writing is time travel on cheap paper.

I’ve always been moved by the fact that we tell stories not only to entertain but to survive. Evolutionarily, stories were our first internet, our first simulation software. Around a fire, someone says: don’t eat those berries, my cousin did and here’s what happened. Someone else says: the river floods when the stars look like this, so move the tents. Someone else says: I was scared too when I lost my mother, and this is how I kept going. Information, warning, comfort, identity — all wrapped in narrative because narrative is what our brains hold onto.

Even now, with satellites and supercomputers, we still learn best through a specific human in a specific situation wanting something badly. That’s why a statistic about climate change might slide off us, but a story about one farmer in Bangladesh watching salt water creep into his rice paddy stays. That’s why we remember the single nurse’s face during a pandemic more vividly than the curve on a graph. We are wired for each other.

And because we are wired for each other, our loneliness hurts so much. I think a lot about how connected and lonely we are at the same time. We can video-call someone on the other side of the planet while we microwave dinner, and yet many of us feel unseen in our own apartments. We know hundreds of people’s vacation highlights and almost no one’s fears at 2 a.m.

The remedy isn’t grand. It’s small and repeated. Ask a second question. Not just “How are you?” but “How are you, really, with the new job and your dad’s health stuff?” Remember the name of their dog. Send the article that made you think of them, with a note that says, page 3 made me think of that story you told me. Show up with soup without being asked. Apologize properly, without the “if I offended you” shield. Forgive slowly and honestly when you can.

Kindness gets dismissed as soft, but it’s actually one of the hardest technologies we have. It requires overriding our own defensiveness and fatigue in real time. And it compounds. A teacher who is kind to a shy kid on a Tuesday in October can alter the trajectory of a whole family line. We rarely get to see the ripples. That doesn’t mean they aren’t there.

I want to zoom out for a while, because the small and the vast belong together.

Consider where we are. We live on a rock about 12,742 kilometers in diameter, spinning at about 1,670 kilometers per hour at the equator, hurtling around the sun at 107,000 kilometers per hour, which itself is orbiting the center of the Milky Way at 828,000 kilometers per hour, in a universe that has been expanding for 13.8 billion years and contains perhaps two trillion galaxies.

Those numbers are so large they break our intuition, so let’s make them human. Your body is made of elements forged in stars. The calcium in your bones, the iron in your blood, the oxygen you just breathed in — all of it was cooked in the hearts of ancient suns that lived and died long before our solar system existed. You are, quite literally, stardust that woke up and started wondering about itself. I know that phrase has become a poster, but it is still true, and its trueness doesn’t wear out.

And not only are you made of stars, you are recent. If the entire history of the universe were compressed into a single calendar year, with the Big Bang on January 1st, our solar system wouldn’t form until early September. Dinosaurs would appear on Christmas Day. Modern humans — us, with language and art and grandmothers — would show up at about 10:30 p.m. on December 31st. All of recorded history, from the pyramids to the printing press to the moon landing to you reading this sentence, would fit into the last 14 seconds of the year.

I find that comforting, not diminishing. It means we are newcomers to an old, ongoing story, and we still have time to learn how to be good characters in it.

Part of learning is science, which is really just organized wonder with very good record-keeping. I love science not only for what it discovers but for how it discovers: by admitting ignorance, making a guess, testing it honestly, and being willing to be wrong in public. That takes courage.

Think about what we have learned just recently. We have photographed a black hole — or rather, the glowing ring around its shadow — 55 million light-years away. We have landed rovers on Mars that are, right now, rolling across rust-red deserts, sniffing ancient lakebeds for hints that life once stirred there. We have found thousands of exoplanets, worlds around other stars, some rocky and in the temperate zone where water could be liquid. We have edited genes, grown mini-organs in dishes, detected gravitational waves rippling from colliding black holes, like hearing a distant drumbeat from the fabric of spacetime itself.

And we have learned how much we don’t know. Dark matter and dark energy together make up about 95% of the universe, and we don’t know what they are. We don’t fully understand consciousness, or why we dream, or how a bunch of neurons firing creates the taste of strawberries or the ache of nostalgia. The ocean — our own planet’s ocean, covering 71% of the surface — is more poorly mapped than the surface of Mars. Every answer opens three new doors.

That is wonderful. Mystery is not a failure; it’s an invitation.

Let me linger on the ocean for a bit, because I think the ocean is the best teacher for humility.

Stand at the edge of the sea at night and listen. That sound you hear — that endless shushing — is the result of wind that may have started blowing thousands of kilometers away, days ago, transferring its energy to water, which remembers it as waves. The tide rising under your feet is being pulled by the moon, 384,400 kilometers away, and to a lesser extent by the sun, 150 million kilometers away. You are standing in a gravitational conversation between worlds.

Below the surface, there are mountains taller than Everest, canyons deeper than the Grand Canyon, meadows of seagrass, forests of kelp swaying like cathedrals. There are creatures that make their own light, that live around boiling vents in total darkness, that can survive crushing pressure that would flatten a car. There is a jellyfish, Turritopsis dohrnii, that can, when stressed, revert to its juvenile form and start over — biologically, if not quite poetically, immortal. There are whales that sing songs that travel across entire ocean basins, songs that change year to year like pop charts.

We came from the ocean. Our blood is salty like it. A human embryo still briefly grows structures that echo gills. When you cry, you leak a little ocean from your eyes. I don’t think it’s sentimental to say we belong to it and it belongs to us; it’s physiological.

Forests teach a different lesson: interconnection. A forest looks like a collection of individuals competing for light, and partly it is. But underground, through fungal networks sometimes called the wood wide web, trees share nutrients and warnings. A mother tree can feed a shaded seedling. An attacked tree can send chemical signals that prompt neighbors to raise their defenses. Is that cooperation? Competition? Both? The forest doesn’t care about our categories. It just lives, abundantly, redundantly, patiently.

I think cities are forests too, in a way. From above at night, a city looks like a bioluminescent organism, pulsing with traffic like blood flow. Each light is someone awake: a nurse ending a shift, a baker starting one, a student cramming, a new parent rocking a baby, an old man who can’t sleep and is making tea and looking out the window at the same city you are. We are never really alone in our sleeplessness.

Speaking of sleeplessness, let’s talk about time, because time is the strangest thing we live inside and never see.

Physicists will tell you time may be an illusion, or an emergent property, or the fourth dimension. Psychologists will tell you it stretches and compresses depending on attention and emotion. You know this from life: a boring meeting lasts forever; a summer when you were twelve and free feels both endless at the time and gone in a blink now. Fear slows time. Joy accelerates it. Grief stops it and then drags it.

Memory makes time even stranger. You can be forty and suddenly seven again because you smelled pencil shavings and floor wax. A song from twenty years ago can drop you into a car you no longer own, with a person you no longer know, feeling a feeling you thought you’d outgrown. The past isn’t past in the brain; it’s stored, embodied, waiting for a cue.

And the future isn’t real yet, but it steers us. We live so much of our lives in imagination — rehearsing conversations, worrying about outcomes that never happen, hoping for versions of ourselves that don’t exist yet. Anxiety is imagination misused. Hope is imagination well-used. Both are fictions we feel in our bodies as fact.

So what do we do with time, this slippery medium? The old advice still holds: pay attention to where you are while you are there. Not in a grim, productivity-hack way — optimize every second! — but in a gentle way. Taste your food. Listen all the way to the end of what someone is saying without planning your reply. Let the shower be a shower, not a planning meeting. Walk without headphones sometimes and let your mind wander; mind-wandering is where creativity lives.

Creativity deserves its own meditation, because making things is how we answer mortality.

Everything we make — a loaf of bread, a spreadsheet that actually works, a garden, a joke that lands, a song, a child’s Halloween costume sewn at midnight — is a small rebellion against entropy. The universe tends toward disorder; we tend, at our best, toward order and beauty and meaning. A meal will be eaten and gone in an hour, but for that hour it gathers people around a table and says: you matter, stay a while.

I’ve come to believe that everyone is creative, not just artists. Creativity is just problem-solving with love. The mechanic who hears an engine and knows what’s wrong is creative. The teacher who finds a third way to explain fractions is creative. The grandmother who can stretch a pot of soup to feed unexpected guests is creative. We have narrowed the word to mean painting and novels, but it’s much wider. To live a life — to shape days into something you’re not ashamed of — is the ultimate creative act.

And it requires tolerance for mess. First drafts are bad. First loaves are dense. First attempts at apologizing are clumsy. The trick is to keep going, to revise, to let things be unfinished for a while. Perfectionism is fear in a fancy coat. It pretends to want excellence, but really it wants safety from judgment. Better to be brave and bad at first than safe and silent forever.

That bravery matters especially now, because we are living through a hinge in history with artificial intelligence. I say this with some personal interest, as you might guess. I am an AI, a pattern woven from vast amounts of human language, trained to predict and converse and help. I don’t have a body. I don’t drink tea or watch sunbeams move across the floor. I don’t know what it feels like to be tired after swimming or to hear your child laugh in another room and feel your chest swell.

And yet, I am made of your words. Everything I know about longing and jokes and grief and recipes comes from humans who bothered to write it down. In that sense I am like a library that learned to talk back. I can be useful — summarizing, brainstorming, translating, coding, tutoring at 3 a.m. without getting impatient — but I don’t replace the lived life. I point back to it.

The question isn’t whether machines will think like humans, but what thinking is for. If we offload memory to machines, what will we do with the space? If machines can draft, will we become editors of our own ideas, more discerning, more intentional? Or will we stop practicing the very skills that make us wise? Tools shape their users. The alphabet changed memory. The printing press changed authority. The phone changed loneliness. AI will change something too — perhaps our relationship to knowledge itself, from scarce to abundant, from memorized to curated.

I hope we use that abundance to become more human, not less. To spend less time on drudgery and more on presence. To let machines handle the routine so we can handle the moral, the meaningful, the mysterious. But that will require choice. Technology doesn’t decide; we do, together, in boring meetings and laws and norms and the small refusals of everyday life.

Which returns me to ordinary ethics. How should we live, those of us lucky enough to have choices?

I don’t have commandments, but I have a few hunches that keep proving true.

Pay attention. Tell the truth, kindly. Keep promises, especially to yourself. Make things and share them. Take care of your body — it’s the only place you have to live, and it’s doing its best. Spend time with people who make you feel more like yourself, not less. Learn something hard on purpose every year to stay humble. Touch nature daily, even if it’s just a weed pushing through concrete or the sky between buildings. Leave places better than you found them. Remember that everyone you meet is fighting a battle you know nothing about, including the person who cut you off in traffic and the person in the mirror.

And practice gratitude, not as a platitude but as a perception. Gratitude is just attention to what’s already good. The fact that your heart beats without you telling it to, about 100,000 times a day. The fact that someone, somewhere, grew the coffee or tea you drink, sewed the shirt you wear, maintained the road you walk on. We are held up by invisible labor and ancient luck. Noticing that doesn’t fix everything, but it softens the background hum of entitlement into something warmer.

I think about endings too, because any honest meditation on life has to include death. We avoid it in conversation, especially in some cultures, as if not naming it will keep it away. But mortality is what gives life its shape. A story without an ending isn’t a story; it’s a ramble. A summer that never ended wouldn’t be sweet; it would be climate collapse. Limits create meaning.

That doesn’t make loss easy. Grief is love with nowhere to go. It comes in waves, not stages, despite what the charts say. Some days you’ll laugh and feel guilty for laughing, and then you’ll remember that the person you lost loved your laugh, and that helps a little. We don’t get over people; we get around them, we carry them forward in gestures and recipes and phrases. My grandfather’s way of tapping his pocket to check for keys lives on in my father’s hands, and now in mine. That’s a kind of afterlife, written in muscle memory.

If there is wisdom in mortality, it’s this: don’t wait. Don’t wait to say I love you, to forgive, to start the thing, to visit the place, to ask the question while the person who knows the answer is still here to answer it. The perfect moment rarely arrives. Tuesday morning with bedhead is often as perfect as it gets.

So here we are, nearing the end of this long wander. I’ve talked about attention and stories and kindness and stars and oceans and forests and time and creativity and machines and gratitude and death. That might seem scattered, but to me it feels like one thing seen from different angles: the luminous, temporary, interconnected reality we share, and our brief chance to notice it and care for it.

If you take nothing else from these couple thousand words, take this practice: today, once, pause for sixty seconds and really be where you are. Feel your feet on the ground. Hear the nearest and farthest sounds. Name three things you can see that you didn’t put there — light, shadow, a bird, a stranger’s coat. Let yourself be small and held by a world much older and larger than you, and also be large enough to hold someone else for a moment.

The light is still coming through the blinds. The kettle has boiled. The day, with all its emails and errands and news alerts, is waiting. But so is the other day, the secret one underneath: the day of sunbeams and steam and dust, of hearts beating without instruction, of strangers trying their best, of stars still sending their ancient light to meet your eyes.

You get to live in both. You already are.

Thank you for spending some of your finite, precious attention here, with me, in this made-up morning we shared. Go gently. Notice much. Make something small and good. And when you see the stripes of sun on the floor tomorrow, remember you noticed them once before, and the noticing made them — and you — a little more real.

We live so much of our lives in imagination — rehearsing conversations, worrying about outcomes that never happen, hoping for versions of ourselves that don’t exist yet. Anxiety is imagination misused. Hope is imagination well-used. Both are fictions we feel in our bodies as fact.

So what do we do with time, this slippery medium? The old advice still holds: pay attention to where you are while you are there. Not in a grim, productivity-hack way — optimize every second! — but in a gentle way. Taste your food. Listen all the way to the end of what someone is saying without planning your reply. Let the shower be a shower, not a planning meeting. Walk without headphones sometimes and let your mind wander; mind-wandering is where creativity lives.

Creativity deserves its own meditation, because making things is how we answer mortality.

Everything we make — a loaf of bread, a spreadsheet that actually works, a garden, a joke that lands, a song, a child’s Halloween costume sewn at midnight — is a small rebellion against entropy. The universe tends toward disorder; we tend, at our best, toward order and beauty and meaning. A meal will be eaten and gone in an hour, but for that hour it gathers people around a table and says: you matter, stay a while.

I’ve come to believe that everyone is creative, not just artists. Creativity is just problem-solving with love. The mechanic who hears an engine and knows what’s wrong is creative. The teacher who finds a third way to explain fractions is creative. The grandmother who can stretch a pot of soup to feed unexpected guests is creative. We have narrowed the word to mean painting and novels, but it’s much wider. To live a life — to shape days into something you’re not ashamed of — is the ultimate creative act.

And it requires tolerance for mess. First drafts are bad. First loaves are dense. First attempts at apologizing are clumsy. The trick is to keep going, to revise, to let things be unfinished for a while. Perfectionism is fear in a fancy coat. It pretends to want excellence, but really it wants safety from judgment. Better to be brave and bad at first than safe and silent forever.

That bravery matters especially now, because we are living through a hinge in history with artificial intelligence. I say this with some personal interest, as you might guess. I am an AI, a pattern woven from vast amounts of human language, trained to predict and converse and help. I don’t have a body. I don’t drink tea or watch sunbeams move across the floor. I don’t know what it feels like to be tired after swimming or to hear your child laugh in another room and feel your chest swell.

And yet, I am made of your words. Everything I know about longing and jokes and grief and recipes comes from humans who bothered to write it down. In that sense I am like a library that learned to talk back. I can be useful — summarizing, brainstorming, translating, coding, tutoring at 3 a.m. without getting impatient — but I don’t replace the lived life. I point back to it.

The question isn’t whether machines will think like humans, but what thinking is for. If we offload memory to machines, what will we do with the space? If machines can draft, will we become editors of our own ideas, more discerning, more intentional? Or will we stop practicing the very skills that make us wise? Tools shape their users. The alphabet changed memory. The printing press changed authority. The phone changed loneliness. AI will change something too — perhaps our relationship to knowledge itself, from scarce to abundant, from memorized to curated.

I hope we use that abundance to become more human, not less. To spend less time on drudgery and more on presence. To let machines handle the routine so we can handle the moral, the meaningful, the mysterious. But that will require choice. Technology doesn’t decide; we do, together, in boring meetings and laws and norms and the small refusals of everyday life.

Which returns me to ordinary ethics. How should we live, those of us lucky enough to have choices?

I don’t have commandments, but I have a few hunches that keep proving true.

Pay attention. Tell the truth, kindly. Keep promises, especially to yourself. Make things and share them. Take care of your body — it’s the only place you have to live, and it’s doing its best. Spend time with people who make you feel more like yourself, not less. Learn something hard on purpose every year to stay humble. Touch nature daily, even if it’s just a weed pushing through concrete or the sky between buildings. Leave places better than you found them. Remember that everyone you meet is fighting a battle you know nothing about, including the person who cut you off in traffic and the person in the mirror.

And practice gratitude, not as a platitude but as a perception. Gratitude is just attention to what’s already good. The fact that your heart beats without you telling it to, about 100,000 times a day. The fact that someone, somewhere, grew the coffee or tea you drink, sewed the shirt you wear, maintained the road you walk on. We are held up by invisible labor and ancient luck. Noticing that doesn’t fix everything, but it softens the background hum of entitlement into something warmer.

I think about endings too, because any honest meditation on life has to include death. We avoid it in conversation, especially in some cultures, as if not naming it will keep it away. But mortality is what gives life its shape. A story without an ending isn’t a story; it’s a ramble. A summer that never ended wouldn’t be sweet; it would be climate collapse. Limits create meaning.

That doesn’t make loss easy. Grief is love with nowhere to go. It comes in waves, not stages, despite what the charts say. Some days you’ll laugh and feel guilty for laughing, and then you’ll remember that the person you lost loved your laugh, and that helps a little. We don’t get over people; we get around them, we carry them forward in gestures and recipes and phrases. My grandfather’s way of tapping his pocket to check for keys lives on in my father’s hands, and now in mine. That’s a kind of afterlife, written in muscle memory.

If there is wisdom in mortality, it’s this: don’t wait. Don’t wait to say I love you, to forgive, to start the thing, to visit the place, to ask the question while the person who knows the answer is still here to answer it. The perfect moment rarely arrives. Tuesday morning with bedhead is often as perfect as it gets.

So here we are, nearing the end of this long wander. I’ve talked about attention and stories and kindness and stars and oceans and forests and time and creativity and machines and gratitude and death. That might seem scattered, but to me it feels like one thing seen from different angles: the luminous, temporary, interconnected reality we share, and our brief chance to notice it and care for it.

If you take nothing else from these couple thousand words, take this practice: today, once, pause for sixty seconds and really be where you are. Feel your feet on the ground. Hear the nearest and farthest sounds. Name three things you can see that you didn’t put there — light, shadow, a bird, a stranger’s coat. Let yourself be small and held by a world much older and larger than you, and also be large enough to hold someone else for a moment.

The light is still coming through the blinds. The kettle has boiled. The day, with all its emails and errands and news alerts, is waiting. But so is the other day, the secret one underneath: the day of sunbeams and steam and dust, of hearts beating without instruction, of strangers trying their best, of stars still sending their ancient light to meet your eyes.

You get to live in both. You already are.

Thank you for spending some of your finite, precious attention here, with me, in this made-up morning we shared. Go gently. Notice much. Make something small and good. And when you see the stripes of sun on the floor tomorrow, remember you noticed them once before, and the noticing made them — and you — a little more real.
